title: The Teacher Isn't Always the Problem. But the Teacher Still Has to Change.
author: Jo Lein
summary: Jo Lein argues that an explanation is not an intervention. She describes a familiar coaching loop in which a leader observes a lesson, gives accurate feedback, sends a resource and a model video, and returns two weeks later to find the same teacher talk, at which point leaders start writing stories that the teacher is resistant or overwhelmed while the instruction has not changed. Each possible cause, whether not knowing how, needing practice, not believing it will work, or impossible conditions, calls for a different response, so deciding too quickly stops leaders being curious. Drawing on her book Burn the Script, she suggests that what looks like resistance may be protection shaped by past experiences with people, power and circumstance. Curiosity does not replace accountability but makes it more precise. She then turns on leaders, naming overcompensating, detaching and surrendering as three ways of managing the leader's own discomfort instead of helping someone grow.
points: An explanation for why change has not happened feels like progress but leaves the instruction exactly as it was, so leaders need an actual intervention.
Different diagnoses, such as lacking the skill, needing practice, doubting the strategy or facing impossible conditions, each require a different leader response.
What looks like teacher resistance may be protection, which is a reason to stay curious rather than to excuse the lack of change.
Curiosity makes accountability more precise rather than replacing it, and the wrong kind of help, such as resources when practice is needed, is just busyness.
Leaders have their own scripts of overcompensating, detaching or surrendering, and each one manages the leader's discomfort rather than building someone else's capacity.
quotes: A teacher can do their absolute best and still not do what students need. And a school leader can do everything they’re supposed to do and still not help that teacher get better.
We’ve spent two weeks collecting explanations for why something isn’t working. We’ve been supportive. We’ve been understanding. We’ve even been frustrated.
If we decide too quickly that the teacher is resistant or the system is broken, we stop being curious about what would actually help.
The point isn’t to psychoanalyze teachers. It’s to recognize that what looks like resistance might be protection.
Curiosity doesn’t replace accountability. It makes accountability more precise.

It’s also occasionally a very sophisticated way of avoiding the harder work of developing someone else’s capacity. Building the tool is easier than sitting with an adult while they struggle to learn something new.
Three different responses. Same problem. I’m managing my own discomfort instead of helping someone else grow.
Sometimes the script we need to burn isn’t the teacher’s. It’s ours.
